title: Draw the Light, Not the Asset
principle: Draw the light an asset reflects, not just the asset
why: Everything we see is light reflected into our eyes, not simply 'a red thing as red'; an asset textured with base colors (brown trunk, green leaves) isn't finished.
how: Before calling art done, make sure it expresses the light it reflects in its environment, even if lighting is handled by another team member.
anti_pattern: Making the tree and being done with it.
example: A tree with brown trunk and green leaf textures.
quote: Don't draw the asset, draw the light it reflects.

title: Draw the Light, Not the Asset
principle: Use colored light, hue variation and atmosphere on repeated assets
why: Colored light creates contrast within a group, slight hue variations add impact because light scatters as it reflects, and atmosphere brings depth and distance.
how: Light groups of copied assets with colored light, brighten spots that get more light, vary hues slightly, and add atmosphere beyond plain fog.
anti_pattern: Copy-pasted identical assets with no variation.
example: A forest of cut-and-pasted trees improved step by step.
quote: Colored light shining down on the scene creates contrast among the group.

title: Make It "Pop"
principle: Don't rely on additive blending alone for effects
why: Additive blending pushes colors toward white and gives decent results from simple visuals, but effects then lack impact and contrast and won't stand out on light backgrounds.
how: Use additive layers as support, not the whole effect, and test effects against your brightest backgrounds.
anti_pattern: Keeping the whole game dark just so effects show.
quote: Don't let additive blending do all the work for you!

title: Make It "Pop"
principle: Make crisp shapes the focal point of each effect
why: Adding polygons or simple images and making them the focus gives effects pop; Smash Ultimate does this with all its effects for a clean, anime-style look.
how: Build each effect around solid polygons or simple images, with glow around them.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate effects.
quote: Try adding polygons or simple images to your carefully-crafted effect and making those the focus.

title: Make It "Pop"
principle: Mix dark elements into effects for contrast
why: Effects often look too bright in a scene; darker elements make them visible against light backgrounds.
how: Add darker elements to bright-only effects, and more broadly pair opposites, like straight lines in a curvy design.
anti_pattern: Effects built only from bright elements.
example: Before/after effect samples.
quote: With any kind of design—not just effects—it's best to think about how opposing elements might help your imagery stand out.

title: Emphasize Objects with Collision
principle: Make colliding terrain stand out more than the backdrop.
why: In action games players must always know where solid ground is, and 3D perspective makes collision hard to recognize.
how: Give non-terrain elements less emphasis, for example with aerial perspective, and check that terrain reads first during play.
anti_pattern: A backdrop that outshines the terrain.
example: Super Smash Bros. stages.
quote: Make the objects with collision stand out— and give the backdrop less emphasis.

title: Emphasize Objects with Collision
principle: Balance readability and looks, giving gameplay the slight edge.
why: Some say visuals are irrelevant to gameplay, but that won't matter if nobody buys the game; still, gameplay clarity should get the slight edge.
how: Don't just fade out everything that isn't terrain; keep backgrounds attractive while ensuring terrain dominates.
anti_pattern: Applying aerial perspective alone and hurting the overall look.
quote: It's all about striking a balance, though I'd say it's best to give gameplay the slight edge.

title: Let Your Characters Shine
principle: Keep characters visible inside their own effects.
why: Effects are needed for impact, but characters easily get lost in them, especially in 3D views that aren't overhead.
how: Shape effects so the character stays at least partially visible, like Terry inside the Power Dunk crown or Captain Falcon in the Falcon Punch.
anti_pattern: Effects that completely bury the character.
example: Terry's Power Dunk and Captain Falcon's Falcon Punch in Super Smash Bros.
quote: Though it's tough to avoid if you want to leave an impact, sometimes characters can get lost in a sea of special effects.

title: Let Your Characters Shine
principle: Vary effect geometry by viewing side so it doesn't block characters.
why: Making the parts of an effect different heights from the front and back keeps it from obstructing the character in the middle.
how: For effects that surround a character, shape the camera-facing parts differently from the far side so the character remains visible.
example: The inner blue peaks of Chrom's Up Special.
quote: If you look at the inner blue peaks, you'll notice they're a different height when viewed from the front or back.

title: Let Your Characters Shine
principle: In 3D, avoid forced draw priority; fix visibility with shapes and outlines.
why: In 2D characters can simply draw over effects, but forcing that in 3D usually creates depth disparity that looks bad.
how: Solve visibility through effect shapes, and add an outline around character models.
anti_pattern: Forcing characters to render above 3D effects.
quote: In a 3D game, it's possible to forcibly give the characters higher display priority, but more often than not this creates depth disparity, and just doesn't look that great.

title: A Small Window Into the World
principle: Scale up targets that look too small on screen.
why: In first-person shooters the target is tiny compared with the screen, which lacks some impact as entertainment.
how: Make enemies several times bigger than the player character, as in Kid Icarus: Uprising, if it fits what you're going for.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's oversized enemies.
quote: In Kid Icarus: Uprising, I compensated for this by making enemies several times bigger than the player, but it really depends on what you're going for.

title: Distinguishing Between Major and Minor Elements
principle: Put performance and detail where players are actually looking.
why: Hardware is weaker than people think, and players mostly look at the screen center and the playable surfaces.
how: Detail the area in front of the camera and the stage surface; simplify the rest of the skysphere and off-screen foundations.
example: Super Smash Bros. skyspheres and stage terrain.
quote: But the place players are most likely to be looking is the center of the screen.

title: Distinguishing Between Major and Minor Elements
principle: Budget assets by on-screen size and every context they appear in.
why: Elements shown small in play don't need lavish detail, but models also shown up close in other assets need more.
how: Estimate each element's screen coverage in play, factor in its other close-up uses, then assign its budget.
anti_pattern: Lavishing detail on elements that are small on screen.
example: Smash fighters versus stages.
quote: It's important to consider how much of the screen each element takes up.

title: Flash, Blast, and Smoke
principle: Stage explosions as flash, blast, smoke, then a natural conclusion
why: Each stage communicates something: the instant flash says something intense happened, the blast is the core of the explosion, and the smoke and conclusion show where it took place.
how: Start with an instant flash whose rays reach past the blast range (mix in black so it reads on white), then a crisp blast with sparks, then black smoke as flames wane, then flickering sparkles.
anti_pattern: Just spitting out a blast of fire and calling it a day.
example: Star Force's five-frame explosion; Smash Bros. explosions
quote: That quick burst of light immediately tells players that something intense just happened.

title: Flash, Blast, and Smoke
principle: Keep the hit short but let the explosion visuals finish
why: Clearing smoke instantly would be better for pure gameplay, but a shorter explosion lacks impact and hides where it happened.
how: Keep the damaging hit active for only part of the blast, and let the smoke reach its natural end.
anti_pattern: Cutting explosions short for gameplay convenience.
example: Smash Bros. explosions
quote: Letting the explosion reach its natural conclusion and showing players where it took place is vital.

title: Flash, Blast, and Smoke
principle: Make separate ground and air variants of explosions
why: Explosions behave differently depending on where they occur, and each type calls for its own know-how.
how: On the ground, make the blast spread upward and the shockwave follow the floor; add screen flash or shake only when it suits that explosion.
anti_pattern: Using screen shake indiscriminately, since it greatly changes how an explosion feels.
example: Young Link's bombs in Smash Bros.
quote: When it's on the ground, the blast spreads upwards and the shockwave follows the ground surface.

title: Get the Sense of Scale Right
principle: Fix sense of scale through materials before shape
why: A plastic model shares the real object's shape and color yet looks small; CG naturally looks like a scale model, and shape issues are lower priority.
how: Correct textures, saturation, specularity, normal maps and surface detail first, after the game's atmosphere is established.
anti_pattern: Focusing on the model's shape first.
example: Real object vs. its plastic scale model
quote: Normally, objects made in CG will look more like a scale model, so you have to find ways to make up that difference.

title: Get the Sense of Scale Right
principle: Scale texture loops and detail to the object's real size
why: A texture loop that's too small, or material painted too small, makes a large object look small and fake; normal maps that don't match the asset's scale feel off.
how: Enlarge the repeat and the painted detail (tile spots, grass hue variation), judge it from farther away, and match normal-map detail to the asset's size.
anti_pattern: Too-small texture loops; mismatched normal-map scale.
example: Tile and grass textures
quote: When creating textures like these, a common mistake is not making a big enough loop, or painting the material too small.

title: Get the Sense of Scale Right
principle: Tone down saturation and gloss on large realistic objects
why: Saturated textures are less affected by ambient light and look fake, and too much gloss makes things look like toys.
how: Desaturate realistic assets, limit specular area and strength, add dirt to large mechanical objects, and mix varied hues into monotone plating.
anti_pattern: Overdoing saturation or gloss on objects meant to look real.
quote: Too much gloss will make things look like toys.

title: Visual Effects in Slow Motion
principle: Study effects in slow motion with backgrounds disabled
why: Visual effects deliver a great deal of information in an instant, so they are hard to parse at full speed, and careful observation is a shortcut to success.
how: Record effects with slow motion on and backgrounds off, then step through them frame by frame to learn their shapes, timing and layering.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate effects recorded in slow motion with backgrounds disabled.
quote: Careful observation is a shortcut to success no matter what you're making, so I hope this proves to be a valuable resource.

title: Visual Effects in Slow Motion
principle: Fill your game with plenty of exciting effects
why: Effects fly by too quickly to notice, but without them the game looks plain, and different effects make the same game feel quite different.
how: Compare key scenes with effects on and off; if the difference is small, add more and bolder effects.
anti_pattern: Skimping on effects because they are on screen only briefly.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate with effects removed looks pretty plain.
quote: The same game can end up feeling quite different with different effects, so if you really want to bring your game to life, fill it with plenty of exciting effects!

title: Supervising Art Through Retouches
principle: Enrich flat backgrounds with contrast and hue-shifted light
why: Introducing a complex color mesh to a monochromatic background improved the piece as a whole.
how: Duplicate the layer, boost contrast, shift the hue, erase the shifted layer where light would hit, then harmonize the colors.
anti_pattern: Understated, monochrome palettes.
example: His Photoshop retouch of the Spirits cave gave the purple layer a reflective glow.
quote: By introducing a complex color mesh to the monochromatic background, we improved the piece as a whole

title: Supervising Art Through Retouches
principle: Keep bright glowing elements from straining the eyes
why: He wanted more contrast and heat on a World of Light pathway but avoided making the magma too bright so it wouldn't be hard on the eyes.
how: Raise contrast to sell heat while capping the brightness of large glowing areas.
anti_pattern: Overly bright magma or glow.
example: World of Light pathway magma.
quote: I avoided making the magma too bright so it wouldn't be hard on the eyes.

title: Praise the Player!
principle: Shape celebrations to heighten how the scoring player feels
why: Smash Ultimate's KO confetti may seem odd for the player who erred, but it colorfully praises the one who scored; praise should match or heighten the player's feelings rather than being the most obvious expression.
how: Add colorful celebratory effects to the scoring moment, aimed at the player who earned it.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: confetti added to the KO explosion.
quote: try not to express things in the most obvious fashion— instead, try to match how the player is feeling, or find a way to heighten those feelings.

title: An Up-Close Look at Smash Bros. Stages
principle: Study shipped stages up close as environment art reference
why: He presented close-up views of the Stage team's work as great reference for aspiring game artists.
how: Review finished game environments from close camera views to learn how each recreated world is built.
example: Close-ups of 33 Ultimate stages, from Jungle Japes to Hollow Bastion.
quote: it should prove great reference for any aspiring game artists.

title: Posing Suggestions
principle: Fix the fundamental pose before finishing touches
why: Smash Bros. artwork is polished down to the finishing touches, but it all comes down to posing.
how: Approve the base pose first, then judge by eye rather than formula before polishing.
anti_pattern: Polishing art whose base pose is off.
example: Super Smash Bros. official artwork.
quote: If the fundamental pose is off, it just won't look right.

title: The Basics of Pixel Art
principle: Draw small symmetric shapes at odd-numbered dimensions
why: An odd size has a clear center (median) line, so at sprite scale a 15x15 circle reads as a truer circle than a 16x16 one.
how: Draw circles at 15x15 inside a 16x16 sprite; in crafting games with broad units, build symmetric objects with odd-numbered sides.
anti_pattern: Drawing tiny circles at even sizes with no center line.
example: Kirby on Game Boy is a 16x16 sprite that Sakurai drew himself.
quote: If you compare them, you'll see the 15x15 one is more of a true circle. That's because it has clear median lines.

title: The Basics of Pixel Art
principle: Give each extra color a job: highlight, edge softening or reflection
why: With just black and white, an outline and a highlight already distinguish a bubble from a cannonball; one more color lets you soften edges, which is essential for precise detail.
how: Start from silhouette plus highlight, then add a third color for anti-aliased edges or a floor reflection on shiny material, chosen against the actual background color.
anti_pattern: Shading a round object with a mesh pattern, which makes it look flat rather than round.
quote: With just one more color, we're able to soften the edges. This technique is essential for more precise details.

title: Kid Icarus: Uprising
principle: Size enemies for the screen the game is played on
why: Focusing on a tiny part of the screen to hit distant targets suits a handheld poorly, so Uprising made enemies many times larger than normal.
how: On small screens, scale enemies well above genre norms (Uprising's standard enemies are four to five times Pit's size).
anti_pattern: Requiring pinpoint aim at tiny distant targets on a portable screen.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising land battles.

title: Unifying Visual Style
principle: Set the look with a few image boards before production
why: Image boards by an exceptional artist give the team a base for models and lighting, ironing out skill and style differences and pointing everyone the same way.
how: Have your strongest artist paint the world, scenery, characters and items first, and review all assets against those boards.
anti_pattern: Letting each artist work in their own preferred style.
quote: Start with a singular visual concept, then execute on that concept with skilled art. That's the way that countless games come together.

title: Unifying Visual Style
principle: Bridge mixed art styles with shared material detail
why: Smash mixes realistic and cartoony characters; without unifying them it might look like a fight between live action and animation.
how: Add realistic material textures to stylized characters (e.g., denim on cartoony overalls) so they sit beside realistic ones.
anti_pattern: Leaving characters from different sources in clashing styles.
example: Super Smash Bros.: denim texture on Mario's overalls.

title: Hit Marks
principle: Match hit-mark flashiness and duration to the hit's impact
why: Hit marks exist for clear visual feedback and fun, so flashy is generally best, but quick repeated hits need short effects and even long ones should resolve fairly quickly.
how: Tie effect size and lifetime to damage or attack strength; keep multi-hit effects brief and tune style to the title (cartoony vs. realistic).
anti_pattern: Hit marks that cover the characters or clutter the screen.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's range of hit marks.

title: Hit Marks
principle: Include dark tones so hit marks read on any background
why: Purely additive or weak-contrast effects feel lacking, and all-bright effects aren't visible enough on light backgrounds.
how: Pair bright additive layers with a dark element, such as a dark backdrop, and check the mark on light and dark stages.
anti_pattern: Relying only on additive blending.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate hit marks with a dark backdrop.
quote: Exclusively bright effects won't be visible enough on a lighter background, so it's good to include some dark colors as well.

title: Hit Marks
principle: Spawn hit marks at the real hitbox contact point
why: A hit happens where attack and target hitboxes meet; if that isn't checked correctly, the mark appears in a strange spot, especially with large hitboxes.
how: Compute the effect position from the overlapping hitboxes and add layered elements there (shockwave behind, upward spray, sparks for machines).
example: Super Smash Bros.: pulled-back camera means large hitboxes.

title: A Fight Between Live Action and Animation
principle: Unify mixed art styles by meeting in the middle on detail
why: Matching each official design would give an incohesive look. Cartoony characters have flat fills while realistic ones have rich textures, so both need adjusting toward each other.
how: Add material texture to flat-shaded characters, tone down texture on realistic ones, tweak proportions slightly, and give every character the same refinement pass.
anti_pattern: Importing every character's original design unchanged.
example: Mario's denim textures in Brawl. Bayonetta's adjusted proportions. Olimar's suit, R.O.B.'s added detail, Ice Climbers' spiked boots.
quote: Don't make it look like a fight between live action and animation.

title: A Fight Between Live Action and Animation
principle: Mute bright primary colors and let them respond to lighting
why: In games a bright red looks roughly the same under any lighting, which clashes with characters using subdued palettes.
how: Render bold reds, blues and yellows slightly paler and make them more strongly affected by light sources.
anti_pattern: Leaving saturated primaries flat and unlit beside realistically shaded characters.
example: Smash Bros. characters originally featuring big, bold colors.

title: A Fight Between Live Action and Animation
principle: Ground stylized features in how they'd work if characters were real
why: Thinking about how characters would look and behave if they really existed helps flesh out details so they sit naturally beside realistic characters.
how: Replace comic shorthand with physical logic, e.g., have eyelids close instead of pupils shutting, and get the license holder's permission.
anti_pattern: Keeping comic-book shorthand that breaks next to realistic characters.
example: Donkey Kong and Yoshi's eyelids close in Smash. Donkey Kong's teeth fit together differently.

title: Do Graphics Impact Fun?
principle: Let gameplay give environments presence; match art to how players look
why: Environments are just polygons until gameplay gives them meaning. Frequent deaths make players scrutinize every nook, while the same art at high speed leaves a very different impression.
how: Decide how closely your gameplay makes players inspect the world and put environmental detail where they'll actually look.
anti_pattern: Making environment art without considering the game's pace and threat level.
example: Dark Souls and Sekiro vs. a game with Sonic running at high speed.
quote: The game world is a mirage you can pass straight through.

title: Do Graphics Impact Fun?
principle: Elevate graphics and game essence together rather than trading one off
why: Graphics multiply a game's fun, and essence and visuals affect each other, so it's best to strike a balance and raise both.
how: Develop art alongside mechanics and review them together so each reinforces the other.
anti_pattern: Dismissing graphics as unrelated to fun.
quote: In that sense, you could say that graphics multiply the fun of a game.

title: Billboards
principle: Build particles and light flashes from billboards to save render cost
why: 2D objects have a relatively low rendering cost, and billboards suit intangible effects such as flashes of light.
how: Compose explosions and flashes from camera-facing billboard particles, then layer extras like sparks on top.
example: Smash Bros. explosions, which are flat images when paused and viewed from another angle.
quote: 2D objects have a relatively low rendering cost. And billboards are just perfect for intangible effects such as flashes of light.

title: Billboards
principle: Check billboards under camera rotation; use Y-axis billboards carefully
why: Billboards look strange when the camera rotates around them, and Y-axis billboards misused for effects feel too skinny.
how: Orbit the camera around every billboarded asset in review and switch to a model where it breaks.
anti_pattern: Misusing Y-axis billboards for effects.
example: Smash Bros. food items, traditionally billboards.

title: Special Crossover! #3
principle: Telegraph dangerous attacks with clear visual tells players can react to
why: Punch-Out!! signals your chance to dodge when the opponent's eyes turn yellow, while a player who couldn't hear the audio had no idea when Space Harrier's enemies were firing.
how: Give each major enemy attack a visible cue (a color change, a pose) and don't make sound the only warning.
anti_pattern: Signaling incoming attacks through audio alone.
example: Punch-Out!! — yellow eyes signal the moment to dodge
quote: If the opponent's eyes turn yellow, that's your chance to dodge.

title: The Majority Shouldn't Always Rule
principle: Brighten character extremities so their movement reads clearly
why: Sakurai overrode the chosen Mii maid outfit to make the socks white, because brighter extremities make it easier to see a character's movement.
how: Color hands, feet or socks in brighter values than the body so limb motion stands out.
example: Super Smash Bros. — Mii Fighter maid outfit with white socks
quote: That's because brighter extremities make it easier to see a character's movement.

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising
principle: Check that fighters and platforms stay readable in dark or busy scenes
why: Players must see what matters: Sakurai flagged a block hidden by vignetting, fighters lost in Mishima Dojo's shadows (clearer in a desaturated image), hard-to-see platforms and a too-dark costume.
how: Desaturate screenshots to check value contrast, and relight or recolor any character, platform or costume that disappears.
anti_pattern: Letting key objects blend into dark backgrounds.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Mishima Dojo shadows, Castlevania vignetting, Enderman costume
quote: In Mishima Dojo, fighters in shadow became difficult to see.

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising
principle: Honor the source's feeling rather than copying it literally
why: Sakurai compares against the original game when making requests, but the goal is to honor its feeling and do what works best, not to match it directly.
how: Put the source's art or screenshots beside yours and match its palette, saturation and signature poses where they serve the feel.
anti_pattern: Copying source material literally.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Kazuya's knockdown pose and Final Smash; CG movie shots pushed toward FFVII: Advent Children
quote: I don't want us to just copy the originals, but honor the feeling and do what works best.

title: Game & Watch Designs
principle: Work from original source material when adapting a classic character
why: During Smash development the team was given the original Game & Watch LCD patterns as reference, material Sakurai calls precious and a testament to the era's ingenuity.
how: Obtain the original sprites, LCD patterns or model sheets from the rightsholder and use them as your primary reference.
example: Super Smash Bros. — Game & Watch LCD patterns used as reference
quote: During Smash Bros. development, we were given some truly precious LCD patterns as reference.

title: Making Things Look Miniature
principle: Lower saturation on large, distant objects to sell their scale
why: Large objects have aerial perspective, so full saturation makes them look small; the closer an object, the higher its saturation should be.
how: Reduce saturation and let bluish haze build with distance on big objects and vistas, and keep the most vivid colors near the camera.
anti_pattern: Giving huge distant objects the same vivid saturation as nearby ones.
example: Miniature photo demo: raising saturation and cutting blue hues makes a landscape look like a model.
quote: To put it another way, the closer an object is to you, the higher its saturation should be.

title: Making Things Look Miniature
principle: Avoid shallow depth of field except where truly needed
why: People focus on different parts of a composition, and trying to focus on something blurry can be physically uncomfortable; blur also makes scenes look miniature.
how: Remove depth-of-field blur and focus pulls from gameplay and trailer shots unless one specific location requires it.
anti_pattern: Adding depth of field everywhere as an atmosphere boost.
example: In Sora's fighter reveal, a focus shift from background to foreground was removed at Sakurai's request.

title: Making Things Look Miniature
principle: Check scale on the final composed image, not per texture
why: Drawing each material's texture on its own won't produce cohesive visuals, and scale is something Sakurai has to correct often.
how: Review scenes as full frames or screenshots and adjust saturation and blur across the whole image.
anti_pattern: Polishing individual textures without stepping back.

title: Blade Trails
principle: Sweep a fading polygon ribbon behind every sword swing
why: Blade trails are vital; attacks won't have the same oomph without them.
how: Draw polygons behind the blade like a folding fan with the sword as the leading edge, and make the tail translucent so it fades; add similar blur to punches and kicks.
anti_pattern: Leaving swings with no trail at all.
example: Smash Bros. adds blade trails to swords and a similar effect to punches and kicks.
quote: Attacks won't have the same oomph without them, so getting them right can have a tremendous impact.

title: Blade Trails
principle: Use a single flat trail image for one-frame swings
why: When a swing finishes in a single frame the trail only shows for an instant, but hitstop on a hit lets the eye still register it.
how: For very fast swings, show one 2D mesh image of the trail instead of building a polygon path.

title: Blade Trails
principle: Design each blade trail to express its weapon
why: Sword swings may look similar, but the trail can show what makes each weapon and fighter different.
how: Emphasize the edge for a tip-strong sword, use a frenzied look for a heavy blade, match a two-tone weapon's colors, add flames to a burning sword, and skip the fade for a light-emitting blade.
anti_pattern: One generic trail for every sword.
example: Marth's edge emphasis, Ike's frenzied trail, Pyra's flames, Travis's non-fading beam katana.

title: Flipped Animation
principle: Design mirrored graphics so they still read when flipped
why: Text and symbols on mirrored characters or items will be seen reversed.
how: Use horizontally symmetric letters or shapes for logos and emblems that will be mirrored.
example: Dee Jay's MAXIMUM pants in Super Street Fighter II; Kirby's Maxim Tomato built from two mirror images, hence the M.

title: Dealing With Color Disparity
principle: Calibrate team monitors by eye against one shared reference screen
why: Every monitor shows color slightly differently, and measuring devices are of limited use because games are often output on ordinary TVs.
how: Place one monitor far enough away for everyone to see and calibrate color by sight against it; stop using monitors whose gaps can't be fixed.
anti_pattern: Assuming everyone sees the same colors.
example: A Mewtwo image lost its right-side shadow and contrast on one monitor, which no calibration fixed.
quote: But within the dev team, at least, it's good to have a process of eliminating color disparity as much as possible.

title: Dealing With Color Disparity
principle: Light art workspaces as neutrally as possible
why: Ambient lighting changes how color is perceived, so artists compensate and their work drifts off.
how: Replace tinted or moody lights in areas where art is made or reviewed with neutral lighting.
anti_pattern: Moody yellow office lights.
example: A company lit with yellow lights produced art with a bluish tint.
quote: When it comes to lighting, I suggest you choose something as neutral as possible.

title: Motion Blur
principle: Swap in blurred textures on fast-moving or spinning parts
why: Blur shows the afterimage of motion and fills the gaps between frames, making animation feel less stop-and-start.
how: Replace the texture with a blurred version while an object spins, or build blur into textures of parts that are always moving.
anti_pattern: Leaving spinning parts unblurred.
example: Sakurai wishes Kirby Air Ride's Wheel star had spinning blur; Smash Ultimate's Spirit Train wheels and rails have blur built in.

title: Motion Blur
principle: Keep artificial blur subtle and let players adjust it
why: Overdone blur can make things look worse and make it hard to know what's going on, and teams struggle to agree on what looks good.
how: Dial blur back wherever it obscures play, and add a blur-strength setting in the options menu.
anti_pattern: Fuzzy visuals from heavy artificial blur.
quote: The more natural a blur effect, the more believable it'll be, and the less discomfort players will feel.

title: Making Effects the Right Size
principle: Give large effects enough density to read at the right scale
why: A flame as big as a character but lacking density reads as a candle or torch, which Sakurai calls an extremely common trap.
how: Increase the number of flame loops or use smaller, more detailed particles, and give effect artists a reference image of the density you want.
anti_pattern: Big flames built from a few large shapes.
example: Pyra's sword flames looked candle-like until Sakurai supplied a density reference.
quote: As a general rule for creating effects, keep the size of the world in mind and try to preserve the proper sense of scale.

title: Making Effects the Right Size
principle: Spend effect budget on quick, fierce motion rather than fine detail
why: Chasing density eats into texture memory, but effects are constantly in motion, so they don't need to be overly detailed.
how: Keep effect textures modest and put iteration time into speed and motion so the effect looks quick and fierce.
anti_pattern: Over-detailing effects until they eat up texture memory.
example: Texture limits kept Pyra's final sword swing from getting closer to the target density.
quote: The key is making them look quick and fierce.

title: Making the Imaginary Feel Real
principle: Design props for texture, light, weight, use and placement, not just shape
why: Game objects have no physical presence, and a regular table and a miniature one share the same shape, so only presentation and arrangement make a world feel real.
how: For each asset, specify how it catches light, how heavy it should feel, what it is used for and where it sits, then review it in the scene.
anti_pattern: Making something that merely looks like a table.
example: A table with things on it, compared with a miniature table of the same shape.
quote: Take a look at the big picture, and try to make the imaginary feel real.

title: Making the Imaginary Feel Real
principle: Simulate invisible forces like airflow to sell physical presence
why: Airflow is an easy oversight because we normally can't see it, yet visuals, audio, programming and parameters together create the sense of authenticity.
how: Add environmental wind that makes loose objects flutter, and small gusts of wind around explosions.
anti_pattern: Forgetting invisible forces such as wind.
example: Smash Bros.: environmental wind makes things flutter, with slight gusts near explosions.
quote: An easy oversight to make here is in regards to airflow.

title: A World with Less Color
principle: Check color-coded elements with a color-blindness filter; separate them by brightness
why: If a game relies solely on color, color-blind players can't play it, and certain colors tend to look alike across the different types of color blindness.
how: Preview pieces, power-ups and interactive objects through a color-blindness filter (Photoshop includes one), and give similar hues very different brightness without losing them against the background.
anti_pattern: Building gameplay on color differences alone.
example: Meteos: the blocks were checked under a protanopia filter and given significant brightness differences.
quote: If your game is primarily built around color, solely relying on that will make it so that players with color blindness won't be able to play.

title: A World with Less Color
principle: Check art in black and white so backgrounds don't outshine the foreground
why: Grayscale makes it obvious which parts are light or dark and what stands out, which fixes prominence problems before they truly begin.
how: Regularly desaturate background art and full screenshots and tone down any background area that draws the eye more than the foreground; flip artwork to spot inconsistencies too.
anti_pattern: Backgrounds that are more prominent than the foreground.
quote: Background art shouldn't be more prominent than the foreground, for example, and this method can fix those problems before they truly begin.

title: Final Output
principle: Judge visuals by the final composited frame, not individual assets
why: On powerful hardware, post-processing blends the scene together, so it's no longer enough to make polygonal characters look good on their own.
how: Review art with all post-processing enabled, blend hues across the scene, add subtle touches like water reflections, and step back from minor details regularly.
anti_pattern: Polishing individual models while ignoring the whole frame.
example: The same stage in Melee shows a distinct color per object; in Ultimate the hues blend and water reflections improve the final output.
quote: Put simply, it's no longer enough to just focus on making your polygonal characters look good— what matters now is how everything comes together.

title: Storage Tips
principle: Give artists physical reference models of the characters they build
why: For Smash Bros. Ultimate, Sakurai bought fighter models for the artists to use as reference material and kept them out on display.
how: Buy figures or models of the characters being modeled and keep them where artists can see them.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate: fighter models on display, including Pyra/Mythra figures.
quote: When working on Smash Bros. Ultimate, I bought models of the fighters for the artists to use as reference material

title: Flashing Effects
principle: Give character hit flashes internal contrast, not just added white
why: Adding one color evenly raises dark and light areas equally so contrast averages out, and white flashes make characters vanish on light backgrounds.
how: Mix dark or shadow elements into the flash, as Smash Ultimate does, so the character stays readable on any background.
anti_pattern: Simply brightening the character when they get hit.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate added shadows to its hit flash, based on a mockup Sakurai drew for the team.
quote: If you simply brighten a character when they get hit, they'll vanish into the background like this.

title: Flashing Effects
principle: Use distinct flash colors to signal each character status
why: Making a character flash emphasizes a change in that character's status.
how: Assign one treatment per status and keep it consistent: e.g., white for invulnerability, yellow for can't-be-grabbed-again after a throw, rim lighting for damage types.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate: white flash when invulnerable while getting up, yellow flash after being thrown, rim lighting for invulnerability.

title: Flashing Effects
principle: Use brief full-screen flashes for impact, scaled by camera distance
why: Like screen shake, a flash covering the whole screen adds impact through its large area, but a strong flash when zoomed in makes too much of the screen flash.
how: Keep flashes to a single brief moment, lower their strength when the camera is close, and check them on LCD screens, whose response times change how they look.
anti_pattern: Full-strength or long flashes with the camera zoomed in.
quote: considering the impact they add, they're worth taking the time to perfect.

title: All to Destroy One Wall
principle: Make broken objects irregular and check them from gameplay distance
why: Even spacing, square outlines and copy-pasted shapes made the wall look manufactured, and some of these only showed from far away; low splinters also intruded into the fighters' path.
how: Vary spacing and shapes, review at the gameplay camera distance, and keep debris out of the space characters move through.
anti_pattern: Evenly spaced, perpendicular or repeated breaks.
example: Mishima Dojo wall: evenly spaced beams and a square-looking hole from afar; splinters raised out of the fighters' path.

title: Manga-like Visuals
principle: Use non-realistic manga conventions when they express characters better
why: Lacking realism is no reason to avoid these techniques; a mouth moved to the side of a face is unnatural but a great way to express a character.
how: In profile shots, try placing the mouth on the side of the face and judge by expressiveness rather than anatomy.
anti_pattern: Rejecting a technique only because it isn't realistic.
example: Mega Man Legends cutscenes and Sonic put the mouth on the side of the face in profile.

title: Manga-like Visuals
principle: Question inherited modeling conventions; you can't fix what you don't notice
why: Kirby's and Jigglypuff's mouths were first modeled in an older style; Sakurai's requested design is less anatomically true but more expressive.
how: Review models at the angles players see and challenge any default that reads less expressively.
anti_pattern: Taking default designs for granted.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate: Kirby and Jigglypuff mouths remodeled to Sakurai's request.
quote: don't take your givens as givens, and instead look for a suitable—or even exaggerated—way of expressing your visuals.

title: Establishing Characters Through Their Design
principle: Exaggerate silhouettes so characters read even in solid black
why: The silhouette is the part Sakurai would stress most; an ambiguous, unreadable or indistinct one isn't good enough.
how: Fill each character in black, check it's exaggerated and distinct from the cast, and emphasize signature features like hair, ribbons or head size.
anti_pattern: Silhouettes that blend in with other characters.
example: Nakoruru's emphasized hair, ribbon, gloves and legs, and Sonic's large head and exaggerated skinny limbs.
quote: Their form should be exaggerated, even when they're just solid black. If the silhouette is ambiguous and unreadable, or impossible to distinguish from other characters, it's not good enough.

title: The Limitations of Particle Effects
principle: Keep particles short-lived and compensate with higher speed
why: New particles need to appear quickly, so lingering after-effects aren't affordable.
how: Shorten particle lifetimes and increase their velocity so bursts still read.
anti_pattern: Long-lived particles crowding the screen.

title: The Limitations of Particle Effects
principle: Pack several particles into one large billboard
why: Many tiny particles cost too much, so each billboard must be used as effectively as possible.
how: Draw clusters (e.g., several bubbles) onto one panel and make each billboard somewhat large.
anti_pattern: Spawning many tiny individual particles.
example: Steel Diver's projectile bubbles are a few panels, each containing several bubbles.

title: The Limitations of Particle Effects
principle: Stagger particle spawn timing and positions to avoid waste
why: Staggering timing reduces how many particles are on screen at once, and overlapping particles are wasted.
how: Offset spawn times across emitters that fire together and spread out spawn positions.
anti_pattern: Particles stacked on top of each other.

title: CRT Displays
principle: Judge and design visuals for the display players actually use
why: Games of the past were made solely with CRTs in mind, so their art, such as checkered pixel patterns, takes on a completely different texture on modern screens.
how: When porting, remaking or imitating retro art, check dithering and brightness on the target display, and study originals the way they were meant to be seen.
example: Checkered pixel patterns that look completely different on a CRT.
quote: games of the past were made solely with these CRTs in mind— causing things to feel different in certain ways than they do nowadays.

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising: Sora Edition
principle: Mix dark elements into bright effects so they read on any stage
why: Effects with only bright elements are hard to see on bright stages, and layered effects or heavy background atmosphere can bury the fighters.
how: Add dark elements or smoke to bright effects, and cut back background atmosphere that conflicts with the visual effects.
anti_pattern: Layered effects that make the fighters hard to see.
example: Sora's Blizzaga; the Final Smash background's atmosphere cut back and extra smoke added to the explosion.
quote: Effects with only bright elements are difficult to see on bright stages, so I asked for more dark elements to be mixed in.

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising: Sora Edition
principle: Give the same material strong foreground contrast and weaker background contrast
why: Reversed contrast, overly dark character lighting and platforms that blend in are common problems that hurt readability.
how: On each stage, compare foreground and background contrast for the same material, and check that fighters, platforms and projectiles stand out without the floor overpowering them.
anti_pattern: Contrast that's stronger in the background than the foreground.
example: Hollow Bastion: fighters blending into stained glass, hard-to-see drop-through platforms, Greninja's Water Shuriken lost against the floor.
quote: The same material should have strong contrast in the foreground, and weaker contrast in the background
